newsitem.title: CONGO: Red Cross comes under fire in Congo capital.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross comes under fire in Congo capital.

text.p: Congolese gunmen fired near a Red Cross convoy removing corpses from the streets of the war-scarred capital Brazzaville on Saturday, the only serious hiccough so far in a renewed ceasefire.
Three International Red Cross (ICRC) workers and some 40 volunteers going about the grim task of sanitising the city centre streets ducked for cover as shots crackled around them. No one was injured.
The fire came from the direction of a part of town held by the "Cobras", a militia which government forces tried to disarm on June 5, thus igniting the unexpected battle for the city.
"As you can see we are working under extremely difficult conditions," convoy leader Darcy Christen told Reuters.
"It is very tense still near the front lines and we will have to continue our negotiations to ensure we can work."
The mission was abandoned after collecting seven bodies, including an old man and a woman killed by a rocket as they were carting goods past parliament in a wheelbarrow.
Later, a smaller team, equipped with heavy-duty gloves and boots, disinfectant spray and body bags, ventured out again to resume their work.

Hundreds of corpses still litter the boulevards and avenues of the former French colonial capital, which was fragmented by fighting between former Marxist ruler Denis Sassou Nguesso's Cobras and the forces of President Pacal Lissouba.
For 12 days, artillery fire boomed across the city while France beefed up its military presence, centred on the airport, to evacuate more than 5,000 foreigners.
A ceasefire has generally held -- isolated gunshots, explosions and the Red Cross incident apart -- since Wednesday. It was renewed by the warring sides for a week from Saturday.
The Congolese rivals have now been left to their own devices to find a solution to their hostilities.

France, which had helped arrange the initial truce, pulled the last of its 1,250 soldiers out on Friday, ignoring U.N. pleas for them to prevent a power vacuum by staying until a mooted African intervention force could take their place.
A similar mission has largely kept the peace in the neighbouring mutiny-plagued Central African Republic since early this year, but fresh trouble erupted in the capital Bangui on Saturday.
There has been no sign yet when such a force could arrive in Brazzaville or who would take part.
There is also no political answer in sight to the rivalry that has scuppered presidential elections on July 27.
Bernard Kolelas, the city mayor leading mediation efforts, was the third major candidate for the poll.
His spokesman said military leaders from the two warring sides would meet again on Saturday to discuss how to cement the ceasefire in the oil-rich country that straddles the equator.
Only the capital has been touched by the fighting.
Kolelas' forces, involved in ethnic clashes that killed 2,000 people in 1993, have stayed out of the current fight, and their southern suburbs have been a haven for civilians.
Restaurants are lively, markets open and traffic jams clog the streets in his riverside area of Bacongo, while the city centre is a silent cemetery.

Brazzaville is a mix of Congolese ethnic groups, but multi- party democracy that began in 1992 -- when Lissouba ended 13 years of Sassou Nguesso's once Marxist one-party rule in free elections -- has accentuated tribal divisions.
The ICRC managed to collect its first 18 bodies on Friday after a mercy mission to rescue 60 children trapped in their orphanage in no-man's-land, who were brought to Bacongo.
"From now on it's bodies, bodies, bodies," said Christen.
